uses: Fennel seed is a traditional herb for wind and griping: it was added to purging remedies to soften their cramps, and fennel water was part of the old gripe water given to colicky babies. Culpeper recommended boiling fennel with fish, and in folk practice the seeds or leaves were drunk by nursing mothers hoping for more milk. The EMA recognizes the seed as a traditional remedy for mild bloating and cramping, for period cramps, and to loosen a cough with a cold. Its Greek name, marathron, is thought to come from a word meaning to grow thin, and Culpeper says fennel broths were given to people who wished to slim. The leaves, stalks and seeds flavor fish, breads and liqueurs.
taste: Warm, sweet and aromatic, like anise
energetics: Culpeper called the root hot and dry, perhaps to the third degree
caution_pregnancy: Safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and the EMA does not recommend medicinal fennel then, partly because the seed contains estragole, which caused liver tumors in mice. Fennel's anethole passes into breast milk. Fennel is widely used to try to raise milk supply and usual amounts are thought unlikely to harm the baby, but newborns have been poisoned by an herbal tea containing fennel and anise. Not enough is known; avoid medicinal amounts.
caution_medications: The EMA reports no known interactions with medicines. Tell your provider about any herbs you use alongside medicines.
caution_conditions: Do not use it if you are allergic to fennel, anethole, or the carrot family (Apiaceae), such as dill, celery, caraway or aniseed, or to mugwort pollen, which cross-reacts. Allergic reactions can affect the skin or breathing. The EMA does not recommend fennel medicine for children under 4, and only short use for children 4 to 12. Other reported problems include sun sensitivity, diarrhea and liver changes.
caution_duration: Don't take fennel medicine for more than 2 weeks; for children 4 to 12, use it for under a week and only for mild symptoms. If symptoms continue or get worse, see a doctor or qualified practitioner.
caution_topical: Fennel can make skin more sensitive to sunlight, and allergic skin reactions are possible.
garden_harvest_timing: Cut leaves as needed through the season; cutting the stems keeps fresh leaf coming. The aromatic seeds ripen in late summer to early fall.
garden_water: Moist, rich, well-drained soil; tolerates drought once established
notes: A tall, feathery perennial often grown as an annual, with flat heads of tiny yellow flowers in summer. Sow seed directly in spring. It self-seeds freely and has escaped into the wild in places, so remove spent flowers before seed sets. It is a food plant for swallowtail caterpillars, and bees visit the flowers. Dill and dog fennel can be mistaken for it. Grieve records that fennel was hung over doors on Midsummer's Eve against evil spirits, and that Pliny believed snakes rubbed on it to sharpen their eyes. Culpeper places fennel under Mercury and Virgo.
